===== PAGE 1 =====
Vortex filament dynamics and
vortex ring motion revisited
Andrew D. Gilbert
Department of Mathematics and Statistics,
University of Exeter, Exeter, EX4 4QF, U.K.
Abstract
The motion of a slender vortex in ideal incompressible fluid is a classic problem in
hydrodynamics. Formulae for the velocity of a vortex ring go back to work of Kelvin,
Helmholtz, Hicks and Dyson in the nineteenth century, while more recently a number
of models have been created for simulating the motion of slender tubes of vorticity
of general shape. For a vortex tube or filament localised near to a curveC(t), the
relevant small parameter to measure slenderness is the tube radius divided by the
radius of curvature ofC. The present paper revisits this range of classic problems by
introducing a coordinate system closely linked to the geometry of vortex surfaces
in a slender vortex. The motion of fluid elements in this coordinate system has an
action–angle form, and with this the vorticity equation simplifies radically. At the
same time, however, most aspects of the shape or evolution of a vortex are thrown
into the description of the coordinates, and in particular the corresponding metric
and volume form.
As the coordinate system is non-orthogonal and time-dependent, tools of differ-
ential geometry are most easily used to describe the structure of both vorticity and
coordinate system, and a general mathematical framework is set out. This resulting
system of equations is taken as far as possible with only the assumption of vortex
slenderness in place, but allowing arbitrary motions and distortions of the vortex
core and of the curveC(t). The modelling is applied to calculate the motion of a
slender vortex ring with arbitrary axial flow, solving directly for the shape of per-
turbed vorticity surfaces and giving results in agreement with earlier studies. The
general framework set up in this paper is suitable for the development of simplified
equations for vortex motion and interaction in future studies.
Key words:vortex ring, vortex dynamics, differential geometry, Euler equation
1 Introduction
Problems of fluid dynamics are often most naturally described in terms of vorticityω(r,t)
rather than the fluid velocityu(r,t). In the framework of ideal, incompressible flow, taking the
curl of the Euler equation eliminates pressure and gives the vorticity equation, with a straigh-
forward interpretation, thanks to Helmholtz, of how vorticity is transported in the flow. The

===== PAGE 2 =====
long-range nature of the pressure field is, however, hidden in the elliptic problem of inverting
vorticity to give the flow field, using the Biot–Savart law. Nonetheless this is an attractive
framework, particularly when the vorticity is concentrated in a tube or filament, localised near
a curveC(t), or several such tubes, to be transported and stetched by their induced flow.
The present paper is one of a series that applies geometric tools to problems of describing
the motion of such slender vortices in ideal, incompressible fluid flow. The first paper (Childress
& Gilbert, 2021) described area waves (Lundgren & Ashurst, 1989; Leonard, 1994; Margerit,
2002) on a columnar vortex. These can be thought of as nonlinear, axisymmetric Kelvin waves
where the cross-sectional area undergoes significant changes. Our goal in this paper is to set up
a mathematical framework for the general evolution and motion of a slender vortex, and future
papers will apply this framework, and also simplify it, for specific problems of vortex evolution
and interaction. We will summarise some background and a few key papers; for many further
references and discussion, see the books by Saffman (1992), Alekseenko, Kuibin & Okulov
(2007), Ting, Klein & Knio (2007) and Marshall (2025).
The classic mathematical problem in the field is to calculate the self-induced motion of a
vortex ring with major radiusR(of curvature ofC) and minor radiusa(of the vortex tube) .
Work of Kelvin, Helmholtz, Dyson and Hicks in the nineteenth century gave the propagation
velocity involving a logarithmic term logR/a; see Widnall (1975), Saffman (1992) and Shariff
& Leonard (1992) for reviews and original references. These calculations are for vortex rings
with axial vorticity, that is vorticity directed along the circleC, but not axial flow alongC.
Incorporating axial flow leads to a more complicated problem addressed by Saffman (1970)
(discussed in Saffman, 1992) and Widnall, Bliss & Zalay (1971), and results in the somewhat
counter-intuitive finding that its presence acts to reduce the vortex ring velocity, and the prop-
agation direction can even reverse if the axial flow is sufficiently strong. Other developments
in the field of vortex rings include higher order calculations (Fraenkel, 1970, 1972), structure
of fat vortex rings (Norbury, 1973), spreading due to viscosity (Tung & Ting, 1967; Fukumoto
& Moffatt, 2000; Fukumoto, 2002), motion of helical vortex tubes (Ricca, 1994; Fukumoto &
Okulov, 2005), vortex leap-frogging and interactions (Riley, 1998), and waves and instabilities
(Widnall & Bliss, 1971; Widnall, Bliss & Tsai, 1974; Kopev & Chernyshev, 1991, 1995).
The natural generalisation from a slender vortex ring is to a slender tube of vorticity
localised near to a general curveC(t), and to ask how the curve, and the description of the
vorticity inside the tube, evolve in time. There is a substantial literature on this problem, and
two complementary approaches. The first is to think of a vortex tube as an object containing a
fluid in motion, which responds to forces on its outer surfaces and which undergoes motion and
stretching according to the balance of these forces. In this approach the local cross section of
the tube is circular and profiles of the vorticity field (axial and azimuthal components) within
the tube are typically assumed, for example uniform axial vorticity, uniform axial flow, and
can undergo only limited changes in response to motion and stretching. Papers adopting this
approach for modelling vortex motion include Moore & Saffman (1972) and Marshall (1991,
1992, 1993), and have the benefit of suppressing complexity in the core dynamics at the outset.
The second approach, which is more closely aligned to the present study, is to make no
assumptions about core structure but to set about a systematic expansion of the equations
of fluid motion about the evolving curveC(t), the aim being to gain equations for both the
internal vorticity profiles and for the motion of the curve. This approach was pioneered in a
series of papers by Ting and collaborators (Tung & Ting, 1967; Ting, 1971; Callegari & Ting,
2

===== PAGE 3 =====
1978; Klein & Ting, 1992), with a comprehensive review in the book Ting, Klein & Knio (2007).
The vorticity is assumed to be localised around a curveC(t) in space, and a local, orthogonal
coordinate system is taken about the curve; the vortex is assumed to be slender so that the tube
radiusatimes the curvatureκis small,aκ=ε≪1. Weak viscosity may be included or not, but
the focus of the present paper and this introduction is on the inviscid case. At leading order,
in these coordinates, the flow is axisymmetric; however naturally the curvature ofCbrings in
corrections of orderεand these can be treated using standard methods of matched asymptotic
expansions, the vorticity-bearing flow within the tube being matched to the irrotational flow
outside. Further developments include higher order expansions (Fukumoto & Miyazaki, 1991),
PDEs for the self-stretching of filaments with short wavelength distortions (Klein & Majda,
1991a,b), numerical simulations (Klein & Knio, 1995; Klein, Knio & Ting, 1996), stratified
vortices (Rodal, Margerit & Klein, 2024), and waves on vortex filaments (Margerit & Brancher,
2001; Margerit, 2002).
Given the wealth of studies in this field, what does the present paper offer? In order to
give an answer, we should stress that much is unknown about vortices when they interact
strongly: for example the numerical simulation of Bustamante & Kerr (2008) shows two vortex
filaments forming a dipole of a hairpin shape moving under their mutual interaction. This leads
to strong stretching, significant deformation of the vortex cores, the shedding of vorticity, and
the possibility of blow-up of vorticity in a finite time (see also, e.g., Pumir & Siggia, 1987;
Pelz, 2001; Brenner, Hormoz & Pumir, 2016; Moffatt & Kimura, 2019a,b). Such vortex dipoles
have been studied in axisymmetric geometry (Riley, 1998; Childress, Gilbert & Valiant, 2016),
where the stretching is algebraic in time, but less successfully in the general three-dimensional
case where the outcome is still unclear (Childress & Gilbert, 2018, 2025). Other areas where
analytical modelling is difficult include vortex reconnection (e.g. Saffman, 1990), complex core
dynamics (Melander & Hussain, 1994) and vortex breakdown (Leibovich, 1978).
Our goal in this paper is to set up models for vortex filaments or tubes that allow very
general dynamics and strong distortions of the core, with only the constraint being that a
vortex must remain slender at all times. We adopt the machinery of differential geometry as
set out in, for example, the books Hawking & Ellis (1973), Schutz (1980), Frankel (1997) and
Arnold & Khesin (1998) (see also Besse & Frisch, 2017), and as recently used in revealing
the geometric underpinning of generalised Lagrangian mean (GLM) theory of Andrews &
McIntyre (1978a,b), by Gilbert & Vanneste (2018, 2025). The aim is to make the coordinate
system absorb as much of the geometry of the vortex as possible, in particular vortex surfaces
are given by a surfaces of constant coordinater. This has the effect of simplifying the vorticity
equation radically, but then throwing the complexity onto the description of the geometry.
The equations we gain at the end of the paper (summarised in appendix C) are still
quite general as the only assumption made in the derivation is that of a slender vortex. To
apply them to specific and novel configurations, we need to undertake further modelling and
approximation relevant to a particular vortex geometry and dynamical process, and this will
be the subject of future studies. However, as a test and to gain useful intuition, we apply the
method to the velocity of a vortex ring with axial flow, regaining known results (Saffman,
1970, 1992; Widnall, Bliss & Zalay, 1971), but with the novelty that we solve directly for the
shape of vorticity surfaces. In this application, our study has points of contact with Fraenkel
(1970, 1972) for vortex ring motion without axial flow, and Kopev & Chernyshev (1991, 1995)
who study the stability of vortex rings to equivortical perturbations using a coordinate system
3

===== PAGE 4 =====
similar to ours. Our coordinate system are also close related to the area coordinates used in
Childress (1987) and Childress & Gilbert (2025), after contour averaging equations for axial
velocity and vorticity.
The paper is structured as follows. In section 2 we set out intrinsic equations for the
evolving shape of a curveC(t) in terms of the velocityU c of points on the curve, together with
two coordinate systems attached to the curve. We write out the governing equations of vortex
dynamics in a purely geometric form, and in components. We then consider fluid dynamics in
the so-calledvortex coordinate systemin§3, which is that used by many authors, in particular
we determin the metric and properties of the background flow, that is the velocityUof the
coordinate system itself. Section 4 concerns the introduction of what we (inaccurately) term
theLagrangian coordinate system: here the surfaces on which vortex lines spiral are surfaces of
constant coordinater, together with an angle coordinateθand axial coordinatez. The exact
equations for fluid dynamics in the Lagrangian coordinate system are unwieldy and so in§5
we introduce the slender vortex limit and discuss simplifications to the metric and background
flow properties. At this point we have a lot of things to deal with, and so to gain intuition
we simplify to the problem of vortex ring motion, including axial flow, in§6. We see how the
equations governing vorticity and momentum lead to two differential equations whose solutions
give directly the geometry of the vorticity distribution in the curved slender vortex, and lead
to determination of its velocity from matching with a standard Biot–Savart calculation. In
§7 we continue with the general development without assuming slenderness; in§8 we apply
the slender vortex limit to gain systems of equations which are the main results of this paper.
Finally section 9 offers concluding discussion, including future plans for applying the framework
for problems of vortex motion and interaction.
2 Governing equations and coordinate systems
Our formulation is based on a vortex filament being localised close to a time-dependent curve
C(t) lying inR 3. In this section we set out the various coordinate systems we need. We then
discuss the geometric formulation of fluid dynamics that we will use, following the notation of
Childress & Gilbert (2021).
2.1 Curve dynamics
The vortex is localised near to a curveC(t) as depicted in figure 1. We will takeCto be periodic
to avoid consideration of any end conditions. We usezas a Lagrangian coordinate alongC
and take points on the curve to be given byr c(z,t) inR 3. Cartesian coordinates inR 3 will be
denoted (X,Y,Z).
Holding time constant, we have the Frenet–Serret equations

2.2 Ambient coordinate system
In the Euclidean spaceR 3 containing the fluid flow, we will use either Cartesian coordinates
(X,Y,Z) or cylindrical polar coordinates (R,Θ,Z) defined in the usual way, and refer to either
of these as theambient coordinate system. In thisambient spacewe have the usual metric and
volume form
g=dX 2 +dY 2 +dZ 2 =dR 2 +R 2dΘ2 +dZ 2,(2.8a)
µ=dX∧dY∧dZ=RdR∧dΘ∧dZ,(2.8b)
and with unit vectors{i,j,k}the position vector is
r=Xi+Yj+Zk=Rcos Θi+Rsin Θj+Zk.(2.9)
We also define a time variableT≡tso that∂ T means derivative at constant (X,Y,Z).
2.3 Vortex coordinate system
Our second coordinate system moves in the ambient space following the vortex centre line
C. It makes use of the Frenet–Serret basis to define a coordinate plane perpendicular to the
centreline curveCat each Lagrangian station labelled byz. This coordinate system has been
used in many studies since Ting (1971) and Moore & Saffman (1972), and is a key stepping
stone to our third and final coordinate system.
We let ˜z≡zdenote the Lagrangian coordinate onCas in§2.1 and write the coordinate
system as (˜x,˜y,˜z) or as (˜r,˜θ,˜z). We use the Serret–Frenet basis{n,b,t}along the curveCas
in (2.1) and set
r=r c(˜z,˜t) + ˜xn(˜z,˜t) + ˜yb(˜z,˜t).(2.10)

2.4 Lagrangian coordinate system
Our third coordinate system also moves with the vortex in the ambient space but will be more
closely adapted to the surfaces defined by vortex lines, as we will explain later. We refer to this
for brevity as theLagrangian coordinatesystem, though it is technically described ashybrid
Eulerian–Lagrangian, as in for example Soward & Roberts (2010). Again we use a Cartesian
version as (x,y,z) or polar as (r,θ,z), related by
x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ,(2.12)
with a corresponding time variabletand∂ t denoting a derivative at fixed location in this
system. We again peg the coordinate system to the centre line curveC; we setx=y=r= 0
andz≡˜zonCas before, so that the curve evolution equations (2.1–2.7) continue to hold.
As we move offCwe allow the new coordinate system to flex in ways that will follow the
vortex geometry. We will make most use of the polar version (r,θ,z) and we set
r=r c(˜z(r,θ,z,t),t) + ˜x(r,θ,z,t)n(˜z(r,θ,z,t),t) + ˜y(r,θ,z,t)b(˜z(r,θ,z,t),t).(2.13)
Here the vortex coordinates (˜x,˜y,˜z) are now taken as arbitrary time-dependent functions of
the Lagrangian coordinates (r,θ,z) subject only to their behaviour onC,

2.5 Geometric formulation of fluid dynamics
We will now set out a general geometric formulation of vortex dynamics, following the notation
in Childress & Gilbert (2021). This can be applied to any coordinate system, allowed to be
7

non-orthogonal and moving in the ambient space, for example in any of those introduced above,
that is (X,Y,Z,T), (R,Θ,Z,T), (˜x,˜y,˜z, ˜t), (˜r,˜θ,˜z,˜t), (x,y,z,t) or (r,θ,z,t).
For the case of a moving coordinate system (the last four of these six) we have three velocity
fields to deal with. The first is the velocity of a fluid element in the ambient space, which is
the ‘true’fluid velocityand we denote this byu. However when we use a moving coordinate
system, a point with fixed coordinates in this system will move in the ambient space with a
background velocitywhich we write asU. Finally, with respect to the moving coordinate system
a fluid element has arelative velocityofv. These three velocity fields are then simply related
byu=U+v. For a steady coordinate system (the first two of the above six) we simply set
U= 0,u=vand regain Eulerian fluid mechanics. If we instead setU=u,v= 0 we have
purely Lagrangian fluid mechanics; the coordinate system follows fluid particles. Otherwise we
have the possibility of choosing an arbitrary division between these two, by allowingUto take
up part of the fluid motion, andvto take up the other part, hence the termhybrid Eulerian–
Lagrangian. As in many earlier studies, the background flowUcan take up the motion of
the filament centre lineCand its neighbourhood, and the flowvcapture the spinning of fluid
elements aboutC.

However fluid dynamics does not take place in the reference space, and so we suppose
there is a time-dependent map Φ which then embeds the vortex in the ambient space, with
coordinates (X,Y,Z,T). The coordinates (r,θ,z,t) in the reference space are pushed forward
by Φ to give moving, vortex-following coordinates in the ambient space as depicted. If we write
down the equations of motion in the ambient space in a geometric form, and then apply a pull-

in terms of (r,θ,z,t) (see discussion in Childress & Gilbert, 2021). In reality, we need not
have introduced a reference space, and we will scarcely mention it again, but simply think
of (r,θ,z,t) as a moving coordinate system in the ambient space. Nonetheless the picture in
figure 2 does show our approach in this study, in particular taking a simple structure of vorticity
at the top, embedded into physical space at the bottom, and indicates the derivation of (2.15).
One application of this point of view relates to the case of a purely Lagrangian coordinate
system, so thatU=uandv= 0 meaning that∂ tξ= 0 from (2.15a) and vorticity is
unchanging in the reference space. The vorticity in the ambient space at all times is then the
initial vorticity at timet= 0, pushed forward by the flow map Φ from time zero to timet,
giving the Cauchy solution to the vorticity equation (see Besse & Frisch, 2017).

3 Fluid dynamics in the vortex coordinate system
We have defined and discussed three coordinate systems in§2, one static and two moving,
together with a fluid dynamical formulation relevant to any of them in§3. The first moving
coordinate system is given by the vortex coordinates (˜x,˜y,˜z, ˜t) or (˜r,˜θ,˜z,˜t) of§2.3 and has
been used by many authors. In this section we write down the machinery, for example metric
gand volume formµ, that we need to express vortex dynamics in these coordinates, using our
approach. We will however stop short of writing down everything we might use, because in this
system the coordinate surfaces, particular of constant ˜r, onlyapproximatelyfollow vorticity
surfaces and we aim to follow themexactly. Use of the vortex coordinate system in§2.3 is
then a vital stepping stone before our analysis in§4 in which we set out fluid dynamics in the
second set of moving coordinates (r,θ,z,t) of§2.4, where vorticity surfaces are givenprecisely
by surfaces of constantr, as expressed in figure 2.

We now have all the machinery we need to set out the equations for vorticity in this
coordinate system, in parallel with the work of many authors from Ting (1971) and Moore &
Saffman (1972) onwards. We will not do so, as our aim is to move rapidly to our third and
final coordinate system in§4. However it is useful to summarise what one can do at this point,
to set related work in context, and to motivate our next steps.
From the point of view of standard approaches, there is the inconvenience that the metric
in (3.12) is not orthogonal in general, that is for curves possessing torsionτ̸= 0. However the
14

===== PAGE 15 =====
off-diagonal terms can be removed by rotating the (˜x,˜y)-axes about the tangent vectortalong
the curve (Ting, 1971). Once the metric is orthogonal, standard vector calculus formulae may
be used if the equations of fluid motion are expressed using div, grad and curl; see for example
the book Ting, Klein & Knio (2007) and references therein.
The next part of a standard approach is to assume a slender vortex, so that the scale
transverse to the curveC, say the radiusa(z,t) of the vortex, satisfiesaκ≡ε≪1, where we
recall thatκ(z,t) is the filament curvature. We should note that we have not used any limit of
slenderness in our discussion so far, except that clearly our coordinate system will break down
if it happens thataκ≃1 during filament evolution. Nonetheless at some point (we will do so
later) slenderness needs to be invoked, and then a vortex is typically posited as axisymmetric at
leading order, so that vorticity surfaces (tangent to the vector fieldω) are approximately given
by surfaces of constant ˜rand the flow and vorticity are dominated by their components in the˜θ
and ˜zdirections. At this stage perturbation methods can be deployed to express corrections to
these base fields in powers ofε, with the usual powerful machinery of asymptotic matching and
solvability conditions (see, e.g., Callegari & Ting, 1978; Fukumoto & Miyazaki, 1991; Margerit,
2002; Ting, Klein & Knio, 2007).
In summary, the vortex coordinate system (˜r,˜θ,˜z,˜t) is useful because the vorticity surfaces
are approximately given by constant ˜rfor slender vortices and that discrepancy, which is vital
in determining the vortex filament evolution through curvature and external flows, can be
treated by perturbation theory. We will leave this approach here, but build on it, as described
in the next section.
4 Fluid dynamics in the Lagrangian coordinate system
In this section we leave the standard approaches behind and adopt the Lagrangian coordinate
system (r,θ,z,t) defined to follow the geometry of vorticity surfaces, as used in Kopev &
Chernyshev (1991) for instabilities of vortex rings without axial flow, and Childress & Gilbert
(2021) for area waves on a vortex column; for a related study in dynamo theory see Gilbert &
Ponty (2000). There are also similarities with the classic papers of Fraenkel (1970, 1972), who
solved for the shape of vortex surfaces for the case of vortex rings with no axial flow. While
the (˜r,˜θ,˜z,˜t) vortex coordinate system follows vortex surfaces approximately, we now adapt
this coordinate system to give our final system (r,θ,z,t), which follows them exactly.
The general idea is summarised in figure 2: we can think of a specified vortex having a
very simple structure in terms of (r,θ,z,t) coordinates (top picture) with vortex lines, curves
tangent to the vorticity vector fieldω, lying on nested cylindrical vorticity surfaces, of constant
r, sitting in a reference space. This vorticity field in the reference space can vary in time,
but any vortex line always sits on the same cylindrical surface. In the ambient space (lower
picture) where the actual fluid dynamics takes place, the vorticity surfaces are again given
byrconstant, but now the coordinate system (r,θ,z,t) moves and flexes. The equations for
vortex dynamics become in large part equations for the coordinate system; essentially this is
applying the method of strained coordinates (Van Dyke, 1975). We stress that we have made
no assumption of slenderness, and the development is exact until sections 6 and 7, where we
will apply perturbation theory, principally to the description of the geometry rather than the
flow and vorticity fields.

We will now work in the Lagrangian coordinate system in its polar form (r,θ,z) as given
in (2.13), where the vortex coordinates (˜x,˜y,˜z) are functions of (r,θ,z,t) that we leave as

˜x= ˜x(r,θ,z,t),˜y= ˜y(r,θ,z,t),˜z= ˜z(r,θ,z,t) =z+q(r,θ,z,t),(4.1)
where we have also introduced the functionq(r,θ,z,t), since the difference between ˜zandz
coordinates will be small when we later adopt the slender vortex limit, and it will be helpful

so that onCthe coordinateszand ˜zcoincide, as usual. The coordinate system is illustrated
schematically in figure 3. The coordinates are pegged to the centre curveC, where Lagrangian
points are labelled byz. At such a Lagrangian stationz, varyingrandθsweeps out a surface
S(z,t), and fixingrwithin this surface gives a curveL(r,z,t) parameterised by the angle
coordinateθrunning from zero to 2π. Whenqis non-zero, the surfacesS(z,t) in figure 3 do
not coincide with the{n,b}planes in the ambient space and so we sometimes callqthetilt.
Fixingrand varyingθandzgives a tubular surfaceT(r,t) on which we require vortex lines
to lie, in other words there is no flux of the two-form vorticityξthrough such a surface, or
equivalentlyωis tangential.

carefully, and this will ultimately determine the evolution of the functions (˜x,˜y,˜z) of (r,θ,z,t)

5 Slender vortex limit
Our development so far has been exact, though we stopped short in our calculations in section
4.3 because the general framework becomes unwieldy at this point. To make some progress, in
this section we introduce the slender vortex scalings, which allow us to write down quantities
as expansions in a slenderness parameterε.
5.1 Definition of slender vortex scalings
In the Lagrangian coordinates (or reference space) the vortex will be given by 0≤θ≤2π,
0≤z≤2πℓwith periodic boundary conditions, together with 0≤r≤a. Hereaandℓare
constants and the slender vortex limit isℓ/a≫1. We will choose our basic length scale and
velocity scale based on the vortex cross section and flow there, and so we will take
a=O(1), ℓ≫1, ε≡a/ℓ≪1.(5.1)
It is convenient to introduceεhere as our small expansion parameter. With this we have for
the coordinates
x, y, r, θ,˜x,˜y,˜r,˜θ=O(1), ∂ x, ∂y, ∂r, ∂θ, ∂˜x, ∂˜y, ∂˜r, ∂˜θ =O(1),(5.2a)
z,˜z, s=O(ε−1), ∂ z, ∂˜z, ∂s =O(ε), t= ˜t=O(ε −1), ∂ t, ∂˜t =O(ε).(5.2b)
Note that we assume time evolution with respect tot= ˜ton a slow time scale, slower than
theO(1) vortex turnover time scale. There is the freedom to introduce further, slower time
scales depending on what is being modelled; see, e.g., Margerit (2002) and Ting, Klein & Knio
(2007) for discussion of time scales and processes.

This means that the flexing and tilting of the surfaceS(z,t) about the{n,b}plane, at any

6 Vortex ring structure and motion
At this point in the paper we have developed the geometrical framework, in particular the use of
the Lagrangian coordinate system, and discussed the scalings appropriate to a slender vortex.

The centre line equations (2.3) remain unchanged under these scalings, and in the previous
§5.2 we have put in place what we need to calculate all relevant background flow quantities
(see§8.1 below). As the general development becomes more complicated at this point, it is
helpful to pause and apply what we know so far to the classic example of a slender, steadily
propagating vortex ring. We consider a vortex ring of circumference 2πℓ, curvatureκ=ℓ −1
and minor radiusa, withε=a/ℓ≪1. We will calculate the velocity of the ring as a function
of its structure, a classic calculation set out in, for example Saffman (1992) making use of
arguments involving impulse, and by Widnall, Bliss & Zalay (1971) using a perturbation series
in the equivalent of the vortex coordinate system. Our goal here is to provide a purely vorticity
based view of vortex ring motion, in a Lagrangian coordinate system, and so insights into how
our general framework fits together. We then resume the general development in§7.

6.6 The effect of axial flow
As our appproach is based on solving the vorticity equation (rather than the Euler equation)
it is of interest to give a vorticity-based explanation for the somewhat curious but well-known
fact that the presence of axial flow in a vortex ring tends to reduce its forwards propagation
velocity (Widnall, Bliss & Zalay, 1971; Moore & Saffman, 1972), resulting from the sign of
the term involving−Q 2 in (6.41). These authors discuss the effect in terms of a force balance
involving the Kutta–Joukowski lift. If the axial flow is strong enough, in theory the direction
of propagation can reverse, albeit that this is experimentally diffucult to achieve and in the
presence of viscosity or other mixing processes, persistent axial motion in a vortex ring is likely
to be short-lived.
We outline the mechanism in figure 4, using letter subscripts for components to aid intu-
ition. Panel (a) is to remind us of the (θ,z) elements of the coordinate system. Panel (b) shows
the axial vorticityω z and corresponding flowu θ for a ring without axial flow, propagating with
velocityV, say. In panel (c) we introduce an axial flow, corresponding to distributions ofu z
andω θ. Now, because of conservation of angular momentum about the major axis of the vortex
ring (theZ-axis), the axial flowu z is stronger on the inner side of the vortex core and weaker
on the outer side. This is depicted in panel (d) withδu z showingu z minus its mean value,
positive on the inner side, negative on the outer side. The effect of this is to tilt the vorticity
surfacesS(z,t) (see figure 3) in thez-direction, as captured by the functionqin our analysis;
see (6.12, 6.18). The tilting (remarked on in Widnall, Bliss & Zalay, 1971) of the curves ofω θ
in panel (c) results in additional axial vorticityδω z as depicted in panel (e). This vorticity has
a dipolar distribution within the ring, creating local velocity componentsδu r,δu θ and giving
29

===== PAGE 30 =====
an additional velocityδVto the whole ring as depicted, which tends to oppose the original
velocityVin panel (b).
7 General development
We now leave aside vortex rings and return to the broader development, to see how far we can
take this geometric framework for vortex dynamics, allowing the most general scalings without
specifying a particular application. We pick up the discussion from the end of§4 and find it
clearest to proceed in two steps. The first step, in the present section, is to develop equations
without the use of any assumption of slenderness. In the second step, in§8, we apply the limit
of a slender vortex, set out in§5, for further simplifications.

9 Discussion
In this paper we have taken a novel approach to a general class of problems involving slender
vortices in inviscid, incompressible fluid dynamics in three dimensions. We have developed a
coordinate system where the surfaces on which vortex lines spiral are given by a coordinate
r= const.and the flow and vorticity have an action–angle form relative to a coordinateθ. A
third coordinatezincreases along the vortex, which is localised near to an evolving curveC(t).
We applied this framework to the motion of a slender vortex ring, and together with matching
using the Biot–Savart integral for the flow outside the ring, regained classic results for ring
motion with and without axial flow (Saffman, 1970, 1992; Widnall, Bliss & Zalay, 1971).
In our geometrical set-up all quantities have clear and intuitive physical meanings, such as
vorticity, momentum and velocity field; the actual physics of the flow is present through the
metric and volume form, which are essential but used sparingly, and no covariant derivatives are
needed. We then followed the general framework as far as we could using only the assumption
of vortex slenderness to gain a complicated set of equations, which for convenience are set
out in appendix C. These include equations for the motion of the centreline of the vortex,
the curveC(t), in (C.1, C.2), equations for a straight, steady columnar vortex (C.3) giving
the leading order local structure of the filament, and then first order equations (C.4, C.5)
37

===== PAGE 38 =====
giving its evolution on longer space and time scales. We showed that this system includes both
vortex ring dynamics with axial flow, and area waves on a vortex (Lundgren & Ashurst, 1989;
Leonard, 1994; Margerit, 2002).
We will now assess the advantages and then disadvantages of our framework, and future
directions. The systems of equations we have developed have the benefit that the vorticity
equation is highly simplified: the axial vorticity is ¯ξ3(r) is exactly conserved, while differential
rotation creates azimuthal vorticity ¯ξ2(r,z,t) and axial flow ¯v 3(r,z,t). Thus the Lagrangian
conservation of vorticity is built in, while the geometric set-up concerns how this is embedded
into three-dimensional space, whether in the early exact framework, or in the later slender
approximation. There is then the potential for vorticity-preserving numerical methods to be
developed out of either the exact or slender systems, in which time-stepping the mapping and
metric are the key components. Both systems require the vorticity to have the appropriate
topological structure in the (r,θ,z) coordinate system, depicted in say figure 2, but otherwise
allow general streamline geometry within the vortex tube as defined by the metric coefficients
gij. Thus, when modelling a slender vortex, there is no need to assume that it is nearly circular
in cross section; the framework can absorb significant core distortions. Although a slender
vortex moving in isolation will tend to have a nearly circular core, if vortices come close and
start to interact, significant core distortions can occur, driven by the irrotational flow in which
each core sits. For example, our framework has the potential to be applied to one lobe of a
vortex dipole where two vortices are driven together in a hairpin configuration, including the
axial flows that are driven by variation in core radius (Bustamante & Kerr, 2008; Moffatt &
Kimura, 2019a,b; Childress & Gilbert, 2021, 2025). The framework also allows the curveC(t)
to have velocityU c of order unity, with reference to our scalings, much greater than theO(ε)
velocity from vortex self-induced motion, and again relevant if vortices start to interact. Finally
the framework could perhaps be useful to analysts in establishing rigorous results on vortex
configurations and their existence and stability, by allowing a focus on the properties of the
geometrical embedding of the vorticity field in three-dimensional space.
Despite these advantages, there are numerous disadvantages. The main one is that the
general framework is undoubtedly complicated even in the slender case. For example, there are
challenges in tracking leading order and first order metric coefficients for cores that deviate
significantly from being circular. Certainly in analytical modelling, the core structure would
have to be reasonably straightforward to allow progress, for example allowing elliptical cores
rather than of general shape. Allowing a model to follow the core dynamics in detail, as ours
does through being vorticity preserving, has the further disadvantage that fluid dynamics
within a vortex core can itself be complicated and the slenderness assumption can rapidly be
lost as axial flows develop (Melander & Hussain, 1994; Childress & Gilbert, 2021). Some sort
of smoothing or averaging may be needed to allow a focus on longer time scales, specific to
an application. In any application there is likely also the need to bring in the Biot–Savart
law, leading to a complex set of coupled PDEs and integrals. Another disadvantage is that the
process of erosion of vortex dipoles, where vortex lines slip past a rear stagnation point and are
lost to a thin layer in the flow (e.g., Riley, 1998; Childress, Gilbert & Valiant, 2016), appears
to be common in many simulations (e.g., Bustamante & Kerr, 2008) but is difficult for us to
incorporate. The erosion process represents either a loss of vorticity from a vortex — but our
modelling is vorticity-preserving — or a secular distortion of the vorticity field which is painful
to track in our coordinate system. In any case, action–angle coordinates become non-uniform
in the presence of stagnation points and erosion.
38

===== PAGE 39 =====
However, going back to advantages and forward to future directions, the framework is so
general that it must contain numerous models for vortex filaments including those already in
the literature, through applying further simplifications and approximations. As such it forms
the basis on which to approach specific questions involving, for example, vortex waves and
instabilities (Widnall, Bliss & Tsai, 1974; Kopev & Chernyshev, 1991, 1995), interaction of
hairpin vortices (Bustamante & Kerr, 2008; Moffatt & Kimura, 2019a,b; Childress & Gilbert,
2021, 2025), and maybe vortex breakdown (Leibovich, 1978).
We briefly outline how one might set about applying our work to study a particular vortex
configuration. First, the general framework may well simplify initially because some quantities
are not as large as could be allowed (for example this was the case for vortex rings, with
U=W=τ= 0,V=O(ε)). We would then need a model for the local core structure of a
slender vortex. Although the equations for this are written in a geometric form in (C.3), the
best approach is probably to recognise that we are simply solving for what is locally a two-
dimensional flow so need to satisfy∇ 2ψ=F(ψ); we can then extract what metric information
we need. We would likely choose the local core structure from some well-known family of
solutions for two-dimensional flow given by some parameters{λ i(z,t)}that vary along the
vortex. Going beyond approximately circular cores, we could for example consider elliptical
vortices maintained by the external strain field obtained by application of the Biot–Savart law.
Likewise a local axial flow could be chosen from a family of suitable candidates with further
parameters in the set{λ i(z,t)}. For example in the most basic modelling one might use the
gauge freedom of settingW c to capture some measure of the mean axial flow, set the rest
to zero, and so simplify the dynamics as done for area waves (Lundgren & Ashurst, 1989;
Leonard, 1994; Margerit, 2002; Childress & Gilbert, 2021). We would then go to the first order
equations (C.4, C.5) and seek equations for theλ i(z,t), making use of further approximations
and truncations. At some point such a model would become a system of PDEs in (z,t), to be
solved numerically and compared with simulation or experiment. We plan further investigations
along these lines.

B Vortex ring motion for general vorticity profiles
In this appendix we revisit the calculation of the vortex ring velocity for general profiles. The
homogeneous version of the key equation (6.26) has exact solutions
f=r −1, r −1

The first of these solutions,f=r −1, corresponds to an infinitesimal translation of the
flow field. It is singular asr→0, and this relates to the awkwardness of describing circular
streamlines about a point displaced slightly from the origin in polar coordinates. Requiring
thatfis finite asr→0 eliminates this solution and pins down the curveCas the geometric
centre of the vorticity surfaces. Note that the interpretation of this solution and why it is
there explains the “fortuitous solution, by inspection, of the perturbed vorticity equations”, as
Widnall & Bliss (1971) describe part of the analysis for vortex core structure in Widnall, Bliss
& Zalay (1971), with analogies to our development but different in detail.
